title: Unit 6: Thermochemistry

topics.name: Endothermic and exothermic processes and heat transfer
Enthalpy of reaction, bond enthalpies, enthalpies of formation, and Hess's law

guide.title: Thermochemistry: review guide
guide.intro: Thermochemistry tracks the energy that flows as heat in physical and chemical changes. This unit covers endothermic and exothermic processes, calorimetry, phase changes, and three ways to find ΔH: bond enthalpies, enthalpies of formation, and Hess's law.
guide.equationNote: Specific heat of water: c = 4.18 J/(g·°C). 1 kJ = 1000 J.

sections.title: Endothermic and exothermic processes and heat transfer
body: An exothermic process releases heat to the surroundings (ΔH < 0; the surroundings warm). An endothermic process absorbs heat (ΔH > 0; the surroundings cool). On an energy diagram, exothermic products are lower than the reactants.
Heat flows from hotter to colder objects until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium). With no heat lost, heat lost by the hot object = heat gained by the cold one.
points: A cold pack feels cold because the dissolving salt absorbs heat from your hand.
At thermal equilibrium the temperatures are equal, not the amounts of heat.
Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond forming releases it.

sections.title: Calorimetry and phase changes
body: Heat for a temperature change is q = mcΔT. In a coffee-cup calorimeter, the reaction's heat is the negative of the solution's: q_rxn = −m c ΔT_solution. Divide by moles to get ΔH in kJ/mol.

During a phase change the temperature stays constant: the energy goes into changing IMFs, not kinetic energy. q = n·ΔH_fus for melting and n·ΔH_vap for vaporizing; condensing and freezing release the same amounts.
points: If the solution cools, the process is endothermic.
Vaporization takes much more energy than melting.
Watch the sign: q_rxn and q_solution are opposite.

sections.title: Enthalpy of reaction, bond enthalpies, formation, and Hess's law
body: ΔH for a reaction can be estimated from average bond enthalpies: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). From standard enthalpies of formation: ΔH° = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants), with each multiplied by its coefficient; ΔH°f of an element in its standard state is 0.

Hess's law: ΔH is the same however you get from reactants to products. Reverse a reaction and its ΔH changes sign; multiply a reaction and multiply its ΔH by the same factor; add reactions and add their ΔH values.
points: ΔH scales with amount: twice the moles, twice the heat.
Bond enthalpies are averages, so they give estimates.

example.prompt: Dissolving 0.050 mol of a salt in 100. g of water lowers the temperature by 2.0 °C. Find ΔH for dissolving, in kJ/mol.
example.solution: q_solution = mcΔT = (100.)(4.18)(−2.0) = −836 J, so the dissolving absorbed +836 J. ΔH = +0.836 kJ / 0.050 mol = +16.7 kJ/mol (endothermic).

misconceptions: “A cold pack transfers cold to your hand.”
Heat flows from your hand into the pack.
It stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.
Reversing a reaction changes the sign of ΔH.

questions.prompt: A cold pack gets cold when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. What kind of process is this?
choices: Exothermic: heat flows from the system to the surroundings
Endothermic: heat flows from the surroundings into the system
Endothermic: cold flows from the system into the surroundings
questions.explanation: The dissolving absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the surroundings (and the pack) get colder.
choiceExplanations: An exothermic process would warm the surroundings.
Heat flows; “cold” isn't something that flows.
Dissolving involves energy changes even without a chemical reaction.

questions.prompt: On an energy diagram, the products are lower in energy than the reactants. What does this show?
choices: The reaction is exothermic, with ΔH < 0
The reaction is endothermic, with ΔH > 0
The reaction has no activation energy
questions.explanation: Energy is released as the system goes down to the products, so ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) < 0.
choiceExplanations: Endothermic products are higher than the reactants.
The diagram's barrier, not the products' position, shows Ea.
Exothermic reactions happen all the time.

questions.prompt: 100. g of water at 80.0 °C is mixed with 100. g of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature?
questions.explanation: With equal masses of the same substance, heat lost = heat gained gives equal temperature changes: the average, 50.0 °C.
choiceExplanations: Temperatures don't add when water is mixed.
60.0 °C would need more hot water than cold.
40.0 °C would need more cold water than hot.

questions.prompt: A hot metal block is dropped into cool water in an insulated container. When thermal equilibrium is reached, which is true?
choices: The block has transferred all of its thermal energy to the water
The block and the water have the same amount of thermal energy
The block and the water are at the same temperature
The water is warmer than the block
questions.explanation: Heat flows until there is no temperature difference; then the net flow stops.
choiceExplanations: The block keeps thermal energy; it just stops losing it when the temperatures match.
Equal temperature doesn't mean equal thermal energy; that depends on mass and specific heat.
Heat stops flowing once the temperatures are equal.

questions.prompt: 50.0 g of water at 90.0 °C is mixed with 150.0 g of water at 10.0 °C. What is the final temperature?
choiceExplanations: 50.0 °C averages the temperatures, ignoring the different masses.
40.0 °C doesn't satisfy heat lost = heat gained.
70.0 °C swaps the masses.

questions.prompt: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 50.0 g of water by 10.0 °C? (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C))
choiceExplanations: 209 J leaves out the factor of 10 for the temperature change.
500. J leaves out the specific heat.
41.8 J leaves out the mass.

questions.prompt: Dissolving 0.050 mol of a salt in 100. g of water lowers the water's temperature by 2.0 °C. What is ΔH for dissolving the salt? (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C))
questions.explanation: The water lost 836 J, which the dissolving absorbed: ΔH = +0.836 kJ ÷ 0.050 mol = +16.7 kJ/mol.
choiceExplanations: 0.84 kJ is the heat, not yet divided by the moles.
The solution cooled, so the process absorbed heat; ΔH is positive.
836 is in joules, not kilojoules, and isn't divided by the moles.

questions.prompt: How much heat is needed to melt 36.0 g of ice at 0 °C? (H₂O 18.0 g/mol; ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol)
questions.explanation: 36.0 g is 2.00 mol, and q = nΔH_fus = 2.00 × 6.01 = 12.0 kJ.
choiceExplanations: 3.01 kJ divides by 2 instead of multiplying.
216 kJ multiplies by grams instead of moles.
6.01 kJ melts only 1 mol (18.0 g).

questions.prompt: While water is boiling, the temperature stays at 100 °C even though heat is still being added. Where does the energy go?
choices: Into raising the average kinetic energy of the molecules
Into breaking the O–H bonds in the molecules
Into overcoming the attractions between water molecules
questions.explanation: During a phase change, added energy increases potential energy by separating molecules against their IMFs, so temperature doesn't change.
choiceExplanations: Constant temperature means the average kinetic energy isn't changing.
Boiling doesn't break covalent bonds; steam is still H₂O.
Energy is conserved; it goes into the change of state.

questions.prompt: A 50.0 g metal block at 100.0 °C is placed in 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. The final temperature is 25.0 °C. What is the metal's specific heat? (water: 4.18 J/(g·°C))
choiceExplanations: 1.79 is the reciprocal of the right ratio.
0.139 swaps the masses of the metal and the water.
0.418 uses the metal's starting temperature (100) instead of its change (75).

questions.prompt: What happens to energy when a chemical bond breaks?
choices: Energy is released only if the bond is weak
questions.explanation: Separating bonded atoms takes energy; energy is released only when bonds form.
choiceExplanations: Every bond has a bond energy that must be supplied to break it.
Energy is released when bonds form, not when they break.
Even weak bonds take some energy to break.

questions.prompt: Using bond enthalpies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol), estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.
questions.explanation: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ.
choiceExplanations: −431 kJ uses only the energy of forming one H–Cl bond.
+183 kJ subtracts in the wrong order.
+248 kJ counts only one H–Cl bond formed.

questions.prompt: Using ΔH°f values (CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ/mol), find ΔH° for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l).
choiceExplanations: −1039.9 kJ adds the reactant term instead of subtracting it.
−604.5 kJ forgets the coefficient 2 on water.
This reverses products and reactants.

questions.prompt: For A → B, ΔH = +50 kJ. What is ΔH for 2B → 2A?
questions.explanation: Reversing the reaction changes the sign (−50 kJ), and doubling it doubles ΔH: −100 kJ.
choiceExplanations: +100 kJ doubles but doesn't reverse the sign.
+50 kJ does neither.
−50 kJ reverses the sign but doesn't double.

questions.prompt: Given C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ, and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283.0 kJ, find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g).
questions.explanation: Keep the first reaction and reverse the second (+283.0 kJ). Adding them: C + ½O₂ → CO, ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ.
choiceExplanations: −393.5 kJ is the first reaction only.
−676.5 kJ adds the two values without reversing the second reaction.
+110.5 kJ has the wrong sign.

questions.prompt: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of O₂(g)?
questions.explanation: An element in its standard state, such as O₂ gas, has ΔH°f = 0 by definition.
choiceExplanations: −285.8 kJ/mol is ΔH°f of liquid water.
498 kJ/mol is about the O=O bond enthalpy, not a formation enthalpy.
ΔH°f is a fixed property of each substance.

questions.prompt: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −572 kJ. How much heat is released when 4.0 g of H₂ (2.0 g/mol) burns?
questions.explanation: 4.0 g is 2.0 mol H₂, exactly the amount in the equation as written, so 572 kJ is released.
choiceExplanations: 286 kJ is the heat for 1.0 mol of H₂.
2288 kJ multiplies by the mass in grams.
1144 kJ doubles the heat, as if 4.0 mol had burned.

questions.prompt: ΔH for a reaction estimated from average bond enthalpies differs a little from the value calculated from enthalpies of formation. What best explains this?
choices: The reaction's ΔH depends on the method used to calculate it
Bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so they don't exactly match the bonds in these particular molecules
Enthalpies of formation don't follow Hess's law
Bond enthalpies include the energy of intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: A C–H bond's strength varies slightly from molecule to molecule; tables list an average, so bond-enthalpy results are estimates.
choiceExplanations: ΔH is a state function with one true value; methods only approximate it differently.
Enthalpies of formation are consistent with Hess's law.
Average bond enthalpies are for bonds in gases and don't include IMFs.
